title: The Kings Emerge From the Mountain
story:
For years the mountain at Girivraja had held more kings inside it than many kingdoms could count. Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had not killed every ruler he conquered. Some he carried home and sealed inside a prison carved into the rock, where men who had once commanded armies and sat on thrones wasted away in the dark, forgotten by the world that had feared them.

Then Jarasandha fell in the duel, and Krishna opened the prison.

The men who came out were hardly recognizable as kings. Hunger had eaten the flesh from their bodies and dried the color from their faces, and long confinement had worn them thin, so that they walked out into the daylight like men who had forgotten what a crown feels like. Twenty thousand eight hundred of them. More kings than most of the world had ever seen gathered in one place. And every one of them stopped at the sight of the dark figure waiting outside the gate.

Krishna stood before them in his own form, and the sight of him was a kind of medicine. He was dark and four-armed, with the mark of Srivatsa curled on his chest, and his eyes were like the heart of a lotus in bloom. His lotus hands held the mace, the conch and the discus; a jewel blazed at his throat; a garland of wildflowers hung over his shoulders. The kings drank him in. They breathed him in through their noses, they reached for him with their arms, and the long weariness of their captivity dissolved in the joy of seeing him. Then, one after another, they bowed and pressed their heads to his feet.

When they spoke, they did not speak of revenge. "We do not resent the king of Magadha," they said. "A ruler swollen with the pride of power does not find what is good for him. Such men mistake a mirage for a pool of water and die of thirst staring at it. We were the same. Our fortunes blinded us, and we fought each other for conquest. See what has become of those fortunes now. You have shaken them away. What is a kingdom, after all, to this body that falls and suffers and ends? Teach us the way to your lotus feet, for that alone is worth having."

And with a single voice that rose from the dust of the prison yard, they praised him: Krishna, Vasudeva, Hari, the Supreme Self.

Krishna answered them. "It is well that you have resolved rightly, you who speak the truth. Haihaya fell, and Nahusha, and Vena, and Ravana, and Naraka. Pride undid them all. Know that this body and everything born of it come to an end. Return to your people and carry on their line, taking happiness and sorrow, birth and death as they come, indifferent to the body, content in yourselves, firm in your vows."

Then he turned to Sahadeva and had the kings attended to. They were bathed and fed fine food and dressed in fresh garments and ornaments. Mukunda himself honored them, and the kings stood before him clean and adorned, their dull eyes bright again. Chariots were brought, yoked with good horses and decked with jewels and gold, and onto those chariots the kings were lifted.

So the twenty thousand eight hundred kings were freed at last from their long hardship by Krishna, and they rode home through the country that had forgotten them. And when they reached their people, they told them everything: the years of darkness in the mountain, the duel outside the gates, and the dark four-armed figure who had stood waiting for them in the light.
reflection: The kings' first words are not curses on Jarasandha but confessions of their own pride; captivity has taught them what their crowns could not. Krishna sends them home not as subjects but as kings again, and what they carry back is not wealth but a story.
next_story_tease: Soon after, with enemies pressing on Mathura, Krishna would begin looking for a new home for his people.
hero_scene: Emaciated kings streaming out of the mountain prison of Girivraja into the daylight, falling at the feet of the dark four-armed Krishna, who stands radiant with mace, conch and discus among the stones of the prison gate.
